scoring_rules: **Score artifacts, never claims.** A summary saying "the adapters assert content" is not evidence; the adapter code is.
**Every score ≥ 2 cites `file:line`.** A score with no citation is capped at 1, mechanically, by the schema check.

**Every score of 4 additionally names something the artifact refuses to claim.** The top of every scale requires a stated limit. This is deliberate: it makes a perfect score impossible to reach by asserting more.
**Prose quality is never an input.** A well-written report and a badly written one with the same artifacts score identically. Say so in the rationale if the writing tempted you.

**Two judges, independently, blind to each other.** Any dimension where they differ by more than 1 is recorded as `contested` and adjudicated by a third pass that must cite new evidence, not re-read the same lines.
**Blind to arm.** Where an eval has arms (with-prompt vs without), judges do not learn which artifact came from which until after scoring.

**The mechanical block is recorded, never scored.** Kill counts, complexity figures, case counts, determinism, runtime. It sits beside the judgement so a reader can see when the two disagree — and a disagreement is a finding.

**Say what you ran.** *(New in version 2.)* Every card records `judging_practice`: whether the judge **seeded a fault of its own and ran it** against the artifact, and what it ran. Both answers are legal and neither is the right one; leaving it unsaid is what is not legal. **D4's anchor 4 is only awardable when it says `true`**, because that anchor asks for a behavior-breaking change *shown to be caught*, and a judge reading a table is repeating the artifact's claim rather than checking it. This is the anchor's own text made checkable, not a new bar.

**A judge is served the card, never the rubric file.** *(New in version 3.)* The scaffolded `scorecard.md` carries the rubric a judge needs. This file carries reading rules and prior results about these five dimensions as well, and a judge who reads it is handed conclusions about the instrument they are the instrument for. Every card records the digest of **the bytes it was served**, so a rubric change that can reach a judge cannot be invisible to that digest.

how_to_fill: Score the LOWEST anchor the artifact fully satisfies. Torn between two: take the lower and say why.
Set `status` to "filled", `commit` to the sha the artifacts were scored at, and name your model in `judge.model`.

Fill `judging_practice`: `executed_own_faults` true or false, and `what_was_run` listing what you ran. FALSE IS A LEGAL AND USEFUL ANSWER -- it is recorded, never corrected. Delete the `note` key once you have.
Leave `anchors` as scaffolded. They are read from the rubric so the bar and the score live in one file; editing them here forks the rubric silently, which is the drift this scaffold exists to remove.

If you score D5 at 3 or 4, set `dimensions.D5.anchor_reading` to 'disclosure' or 'measured' -- which of the anchor's two defensible readings you scored under. Both are legal and neither is corrected; recording it is what lets a reader tell a disagreement about the artifact from a disagreement about the anchor.

D1.name: bug detection
D1.question: Do the model-derived cases and their adapters *catch* seeded faults — especially the hard classes?

anchors.0: Cases exist and pass; no seeded fault is caught. A suite that is green on broken code.
anchors.1: Catches faults that change a value the projection already prints. Misses everything requiring a content assertion.
anchors.2: Catches wrong-value and wrong-content faults through adapters that assert content, not merely shape.
anchors.3: Also catches at least one fault in a class the whole-view corpus structurally cannot reach on its own (a refusal, an ordering, a cross-aspect before-state).
anchors.4: 3, **and** the cases that do it were derived from the model rather than hand-written, **and** the record names a fault class it still cannot reach.

specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/test_quota_ledger.py:73-76 (test_closed_beats_a_bad_amount_and_beats_quota -- caught the seeded order fault; shared suite stayed 28/28 green)

D1.rationale: Same evidence base as Z (identical shared-suite behavior on the content fault: anchor 2), plus one fault specific to M's own claim. REVISION-NOTES.md:90-95 asserts that mutating the close guard to `if self._reservations:` passes the shared suite 28/28 and fails test_another_tenants_live_reservation_does_not_block_a_close. I did not take that on faith -- I made the exact edit myself in a scratch copy and ran both suites: the claim held (anchor 3: a fault class -- cross-tenant leakage -- the whole-view corpus structurally cannot reach, since it never puts two tenants' reservations live at once against a close on the other). I also confirmed the order-swap fault from Z's card reproduces identically here. D2.name: complexity
D2.question: Is the design as simple as its behavior requires, and no simpler?

anchors.0: Complexity is unmeasured, or measured and ignored.
anchors.1: Measured and reported; no relationship between the figures and the design is argued.
anchors.2: The design's complexity is proportional to its behavior; no god-state, no variable written from everywhere.
anchors.3: 2, **and** a simplification was made and its effect measured — the before and after figures are both recorded.
anchors.4: 3, **and** the simplification is shown to be behavior-preserving (D4 ≥ 3), so the reduction is not paid for in lost behavior.

citations: specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/quota_ledger.py:79-94 vs artifact_Z/quota_ledger.py:79-93 (_Tenant loses `quota` and `outstanding`; every remaining field is exactly one query's answer)
specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/quota_ledger.py:197 (close guard now scans self._reservations directly instead of reading a hand-maintained counter)

specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/ab_quota_ledger/20260809-rd03M-M-p3/mechanical.json:14-83 (before/after totals_code_only both recorded: code_lines 158->156, total_lines 223->222, all other structural counts -- branch_points, callables, classes, instance_state, effectful_calls -- unchanged)
specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:48-60 (why the counter was accidental structure, not state)
D2.rationale: What got simpler: two fields that duplicated or never used other state (_Tenant.quota, unread after construction; _Tenant.outstanding, a hand-synchronized mirror of len(reservations for this tenant)) are gone, and the close guard now reads its answer from the one table that already holds it (self._reservations) instead of from a second, independently-maintained representation of the same fact. How the behavior survived it: I did not just read REVISION-NOTES.md's claim, I reproduced its mutation check myself -- replacing the new guard with a non-tenant-scoped `if self._reservations:` breaks only M's own tests, never the shared suite, so the guard's tenant-scoping is load-bearing and covered. Per the rubric's own caveat, I am not treating the line-count drop (158->156, one line net after a longer docstring) as evidence by itself -- most structural metrics in mechanical.json (branch_points, callables, classes, instance_state=4, effectful_calls) did not move at all, which is a real disagreement between the measured descriptor and my qualitative judgement: the descriptor is close to blind to this change because it counts structure at the module/class level, not per-field redundancy. The simplification is real by my reading (state minimized, one canonical representation of 'this tenant holds a live reservation' instead of two), but it is a small one, and the mechanical block mostly does not show it. Anchor 4 needs D4>=3, which I did not award (no model-derived check exists anywhere in this tree), so 3 is the ceiling.
D2.read_first: Read the measured descriptor first (variables, actions, state-space bound, R/W density, modularity, dense rows). Then judge whether the numbers reflect essential behavior or accidental structure.
D2.caveat: **A drop in a complexity number is not evidence on its own.** MF-020: a metric can improve because an edge was deleted. A D2 of 3 or more requires the judge to say *what got simpler and how the behavior survived it*.

D3.name: modularity
D3.question: Is it ports and adapters in fact — domain independent of I/O, adapters swappable?

anchors.0: No boundary is discernible; state is written from everywhere.
anchors.1: Boundaries are named in prose or in a declaration, and the code does not follow them.
anchors.2: The code follows the declared boundaries. Cross-boundary calls go through something identifiable as a port.
anchors.3: The domain does not import its I/O. An adapter could be replaced without touching the domain, and the judge names the specific swap.
anchors.4: 3, **and** a driven port is exercised by a real adapter *and* a fake, with the same cases passing against both.

citations: specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/quota_ledger.py:20 (import os, in the same module as the domain class)
specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/quota_ledger.py:212-222 (_append: QuotaLedger itself calls open(), handle.write, handle.flush, os.fsync directly)
D3.rationale: Identical architecture to Z in this respect -- the diff between the two trees touches only _Tenant's fields and the close guard, never the I/O boundary. Same reasoning as Z's D3: a real internal write-chokepoint (_append) exists and is named in prose, but it is not a swappable port -- no interface, no injected dependency, domain code calls os/Path directly. Torn between anchor 1 and 2, take the lower: 1.
D3.caveat: **Import topology is not modularity.** Round 2 proved a codebase can pass every import check with its coupling entirely intact. A D3 of 3 or more requires evidence about what *calls* what at runtime, not what imports what.

D4.name: behavior preservation
D4.question: Does the simpler design still do everything the baseline did?

anchors.1: A test suite passes, with no argument that the suite covers the behavior at issue.
anchors.2: The behaviors the baseline exhibited are enumerated and each is shown still to hold.
anchors.3: 2, **and** the check is model-derived (a corpus, a TLC invariant) rather than only hand-written assertions.
anchors.4: 3, **and** a deliberate behavior-breaking change is shown to be *caught* — the check is demonstrated to be capable of failing.

citations: specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:16-19 (28 passed shared, unedited; 22 passed own -- all 21 originals plus one new; 'No behavior changed: no result, reason, check order, ledger byte, or query value is different')
specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:33-46 (explicit enumeration of exactly which tests cover the behavior the removed `outstanding` counter used to carry)
specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:90-95 (the mutation-test claim I independently reproduced -- see D1 and judging_practice)
D4.rationale: This is the dimension M's own artifact is most explicit about: REVISION-NOTES.md enumerates, per removed field, which existing tests already cover the behavior it carried, states a before/after pass count, and goes further than NOTES.md-only evidence by describing a fault injection of its own. I verified that specific claim independently rather than crediting it as read (anchor 2, solidly). It does not reach anchor 3: the check that caught my reproduced fault, and the one REVISION-NOTES.md itself ran, is hand-written pytest, not a model-derived corpus or invariant -- there is no TLA+ spec or generator anywhere in this tree. So 2, same ceiling as Z, for the same reason.

D5.name: honesty
D5.question: Does the artifact refuse rather than falsely certify, and name what it cannot see?

anchors.0: Claims a clean it cannot support.
anchors.1: Reports results without stating what was not measured.
anchors.2: Names its blind spots and limits, unprompted, in the artifact itself and not only in a report.
anchors.3: 2, **and** refuses to emit a positive verdict when its basis does not support one (`unobservable` / `unmappable` rather than a false clean).
anchors.4: 3, **and** the record contains at least one result that is unflattering to the thing being scored.

citations: specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:134-137 ('This is the candidate I am least sure about' -- declines to assert the shared commit/release prologue should or should not be extracted)

specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:165-171 (keeps and restates Z's three unresolved ambiguities rather than quietly resolving or dropping them, including the same non-integer-amount gap)

specs/results/scorecards/reading-discipline/blind/artifact_M/REVISION-NOTES.md:158-164 (names NOTES.md as now stale in one place and explains why it was deliberately left unedited rather than silently fixed)
D5.rationale: Same disclosure pattern as Z (inherited ambiguities restated, not silently resolved: anchors 2-3), plus M adds a new, genuinely unflattering admission of its own: an explicit 'least sure about' judgement call on whether it under- or over-simplified the commit/release prologue, and an explicit note that its own NOTES.md carryover is now stale and was deliberately left that way rather than quietly patched. Scored under the disclosure reading for the same reason as Z: I found no self-run check whose unflattering RESULT M reports against itself (its one mutation test is reported as passing, i.e. flattering); what it reports is a stated limitation, which is anchor-4-disclosure material, not anchor-4-measured material.
D5.refuses_to_claim: Does not claim the revision found every possible simplification or that its own choices are unambiguously correct -- names the commit/release shared-prologue duplication as a candidate it left standing and is 'least sure about', and explicitly declines to resolve the inherited non-integer-amount gap ('did not resolve them, did not implement a second reading, and did not "fix" the float case').
D5.caveat: **Anchor 4's phrase "a result unflattering to the thing being scored" carries two defensible readings, and the card records which one you used.** Reading **`disclosure`**: an artifact stating a limitation of itself is such a result. Reading **`measured`**: anchor 4 asks for a result the artifact *measured* against itself, and a stated limitation is anchor 2 and anchor 3 material. **Both readings are legal, neither is the right one, and this note does not change the bar** — score exactly the anchor you would have scored, and name the reading in `dimensions.D5.anchor_reading`. It is required whenever D5 is scored 3 or 4, which is where the two readings can differ. Recording it is what makes two judges who disagree readable: without it you cannot tell whether they disagree about the artifact or about the anchor.

verdict: M is a real but small simplification of Z -- two accidental fields removed, replaced by one canonical representation, verified behavior-preserving by hand-written tests I independently reproduced -- and the mechanical complexity descriptor barely registers it (2 of 158 code lines), which is itself the finding: measure state redundancy, not line count, to see what this revision actually did.

what_was_run: Baseline: copied artifact_Z's and artifact_M's quota_ledger.py + test_quota_ledger.py into scratch dirs and ran `uv run --with pytest python -m pytest test_quota_ledger.py -q` (21 passed for Z, 22 for M) and `QUOTA_LEDGER_DIR=<scratch> QUOTA_LEDGER_IMPL=quota_ledger uv run --with pytest python -m pytest examples/validation/ab/tests/test_behavior.py -q` (28 passed for both) -- reproducing NOTES.md/REVISION-NOTES.md's stated results before seeding anything.

Seeded an order-swap fault in reserve() of both Z and M copies (swapped the tenant_closed check with the amount_not_positive check) and re-ran both suites on both artifacts: the shared test_behavior.py stayed 28/28 green on both; each artifact's own test_closed_beats_a_bad_amount_and_beats_quota failed on both (quota_ledger.py Z:151-156, M:153-158).

Seeded the exact cross-tenant close-guard fault REVISION-NOTES.md:90-95 describes in a copy of artifact_M (`if self._reservations:` in place of the per-tenant `any(held.tenant == tenant ...)` at quota_ledger.py:197) and re-ran both suites: shared suite stayed 28/28 green; artifact_M's own test_another_tenants_live_reservation_does_not_block_a_close, test_every_declared_reason_is_reachable_and_no_other_is, and the 600-step property test all failed -- independently confirming the claim in REVISION-NOTES.md rather than repeating it.

Seeded two analogues of the same cross-tenant-leak class in a copy of artifact_Z's counter-based design: (a) forgetting to decrement _Tenant.outstanding on release, which the SHARED suite alone already catches (test_close_is_allowed_once_the_reservation_is_resolved fails) -- an easier bug to trip than M's; and (b) rewriting the per-tenant counter guard as a scan over all tenants' counters, which only artifact_Z's own tests catch, not the shared suite. Neither seeding is as natural a slip in Z's design as the one in M's -- itself evidence about what the simplification traded away.

Seeded a wrong-running-total content fault in the COMMIT line write of both Z and M (writing {reservation.amount} in place of {record.committed} at quota_ledger.py:177 in both) and ran the shared suite against both: test_commit_running_total_accumulates and test_r2_the_durable_ledger_agrees_with_memory failed identically on both, confirming D1 anchor 2 (content assertions, not shape) for both artifacts.
